H1.text: Stand eight metres from a wall. Walk half the way. Now walk half of what is left. Again, and again.

H2.text: Four metres left. Two. One. Half a metre. A quarter.

H3.text: Diya tried this game in the college corridor.

H4.text: After twenty moves the gap is thinner than a hair. But there is always half left. Does she ever touch the wall?

H5.text: She never lands on it, yet the gap gets as close to zero as you like. That idea has a name. It is called a limit.

P2.text: A limit asks one question. When the input gets closer and closer to a number, what does the output get close to?

P3.text: We write it like this. The limit, as x tends to a, of f of x, equals l.

P4.text: x tends to a means x creeps towards a, as close as we like. But x never has to equal a.

P5.text: And l is the value that f of x settles near. For Diya, the moves keep going and the gap tends to zero.

L1.text: Now watch a real function do this. Take h of x equals x squared minus four, over x minus two.

L2.text: Try x equals two. The top is zero and the bottom is zero. Zero over zero has no value, so h of two does not exist.

L3.text: So we creep up on two instead. From the left: one point nine, then one point nine nine, then one point nine nine nine.

L4.text: h gives three point nine, then three point nine nine, then three point nine nine nine. It is closing in on four.

L5.text: From the right: two point one, two point zero one, two point zero zero one. h gives four point one, four point zero one, four point zero zero one. Also closing in on four.

D1.text: Why four? Here is the reason, in small steps.

D2.text: Step one. The top, x squared minus four, splits into x minus two, times x plus two.

D3.text: Step two. While x is not two, x minus two is not zero. So we can cancel it, top and bottom.

D4.text: Step three. What is left is just x plus two. A straight line, with one tiny hole at x equals two.

D5.text: Step four. As x tends to two, x plus two tends to four. So the limit is four, even though h of two does not exist.

S1.text: Side by side. The value at a point is what the function gives exactly at that point. Here, there is none.

S2.text: The limit is what the function gets close to near that point. Here, it is four. A limit looks near a, never at a.

S3.text: Now you try. Can a function have a limit at a point where it has no value at all? Pause and decide.

S4.text: Yes! h has no value at two, but its limit there is four. The hole does not stop the limit.

R1.text: Notice we came from two sides. Coming from numbers just below a gives the left hand limit.

R2.text: Coming from numbers just above a gives the right hand limit.

R3.text: The rule from NCERT: the limit exists only when the left hand limit and the right hand limit are the same number.

R4.text: Test it. The greatest integer function, square bracket x, at x equals one. Does the limit exist? Pause and think.

R5.text: No! Just below one, like zero point nine nine, it gives zero. Just above one, it gives one. Zero and one do not match, so there is no limit.

T1.text: Remember this. A limit looks near the point, from both sides, and both sides must agree.

W2.text: f of x is x squared for x less than two, and three x minus two for x more than two. And f of two is seven. Find the limit as x tends to two.

W3.text: Step one. From the left, f of x is x squared. As x tends to two, it tends to four.

W4.text: Step two. From the right, f of x is three x minus two. As x tends to two, it tends to six minus two, four.

W5.text: Step three. Both sides give four. So the limit exists, and it equals four.

W6.text: Step four. f of two is seven, but that does not matter. The limit never looks at the point itself.

W7.text: So the limit is four, and the value is seven. They can be different.

X2.text: Find the limit of mod x over x, as x tends to zero. Many students try x equals zero point one and zero point zero one, get one each time, and write one.

X3.text: But they only checked one side. From the left, mod x over x is minus one. Minus one and one do not match, so the limit does not exist.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as functions defined in pieces, or with square bracket x, where you check both sides of a point.

Q1.text: Exam level now. If the limit exists, what is its value? Pause and solve.

A2.text: From the left, a x plus three tends to two a plus three.

A3.text: From the right, x squared plus a tends to four plus a.

A4.text: For the limit to exist, both sides must match. Two a plus three equals four plus a, so a is one. Then the limit is four plus one, which is five.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What does x tends to a mean, in plain words?

Y3.text: Two. h of two does not exist. So why is the limit of h at two equal to four?

Y4.text: Three. When does a limit fail to exist?

N1.text: Next time: a big limit full of sums, products and fractions. Can you break it into small ones? We find out in the algebra of limits.
